trails.trailTip: Snow can linger on the upper loop into July even in a normal year, so check the park's trail-conditions page before attempting the full loop early season; the view of Rainier from Panorama Point is best on a clear morning before afternoon clouds build.
trails.didYouKnow: The Skyline Trail's Paradise meadows sit in one of the snowiest recorded spots on Earth, averaging over 640 inches of snow a year.

trails.trailTip: Hike the loop counter-clockwise from Tipsoo Lake for the best sequence of wildflower meadows and Mount Rainier views; a short section briefly leaves the national park into adjacent national forest land.
trails.didYouKnow: Naches Peak Loop is one of the few trails in the park that crosses jurisdictions, dipping from Mount Rainier National Park into the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per WSDOT, the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge remains permanently closed, so the Mowich Lake / Carbon River corridor that serves this trailhead has no public vehicle, bike, or foot access from that route — reaching Tolmie Peak currently requires a multi-day backcountry approach via the Wonderland Trail, so confirm current access at nps.gov/mora before planning a trip.
trails.didYouKnow: The lookout atop Tolmie Peak was built in 1933 and looks out over Eunice Lake with an unusually close view of Mount Rainier's Mowich Face.

trails.trailTip: The trail crosses Van Trump Creek on a footbridge and can stay snow-covered or icy into early July in many years, so trekking poles and traction help on the steep switchbacks below the falls.
trails.didYouKnow: At roughly 320 feet, Comet Falls is one of the tallest waterfalls in Mount Rainier National Park.

trails.trailTip: An easy, flat loop past historic mineral springs — a good option for young kids or to stretch your legs near the Longmire Museum.
trails.didYouKnow: The mineral springs along this trail are what first drew James Longmire to build a wilderness resort here in 1884, decades before the park was established.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per WSDOT, the trailhead near Mowich Lake has no public vehicle access because the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge is permanently closed — check nps.gov/mora for current approach options before planning this hike.
trails.didYouKnow: Spray Park's wildflower meadows sit near Spray Falls and are among the most extensive subalpine meadow displays in the park.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per NPS Mount Rainier alerts, the White River/Sunrise approach and nearby Wonderland Trail segments have been subject to temporary wildfire-related closures in late summer, so check current conditions at nps.gov/mora before heading out this time of year.
trails.didYouKnow: Summerland's meadows are a reliable place to spot mountain goats grazing on the slopes above Meany Crest.

trails.trailTip: As of September 2026, per WSDOT, the SR 165 Fairfax Bridge remains permanently closed, cutting off the standard Carbon River entrance road — the trail is now reachable only via a long approach on the Wonderland Trail, so confirm current access at nps.gov/mora before planning this hike.
trails.didYouKnow: At roughly 3,600 feet, the Carbon Glacier's terminus is the lowest-elevation glacier point in the contiguous United States, thanks to the deep, shaded valley and heavy Cascade snowfall.

animals.whereToLook: Berry-rich subalpine meadows near Paradise, Sunrise, and Grand Park
animals.viewingTip: Watch a foraging bear from a distance with binoculars and never approach for a photo — give it a clear escape route and back away slowly if it notices you.
animals.didYouKnow: Mount Rainier's black bears feed heavily on huckleberries in late summer, sometimes eating over 20,000 berries a day to prepare for winter denning.

animals.whereToLook: Rocky slopes above Summerland, Spray Park, and Klapatche Park
animals.viewingTip: Scan distant cliff bands and talus slopes with binoculars rather than approaching; during the November-December rut, give goats extra distance since bucks are more easily provoked.
animals.didYouKnow: Mountain goats aren't true goats — they're more closely related to antelope, and their soft-padded, split hooves grip near-vertical rock.

animals.whereToLook: Rockslides and talus near Paradise, Sunrise, and Spray Park
animals.viewingTip: Listen for their sharp warning whistle and watch from the trail with binoculars rather than approaching burrow entrances — a marmot that stops feeding to watch you is already too disturbed.
animals.didYouKnow: The hoary marmot's shrill alarm call has earned it the nickname 'whistling marmot' among Cascades hikers.

animals.whereToLook: Old-growth conifer forest along lower-elevation trails like Trail of the Shadows and Carbon River
animals.viewingTip: Enjoy their scolding chatter from a distance and never offer food — a fed squirrel loses its natural wariness and often ends up injured near roads and trails.
animals.didYouKnow: Douglas squirrels cache thousands of conifer cones each fall in piles called middens, some used by generations of squirrels for decades.

animals.whereToLook: Talus slopes near Paradise and Sunrise
animals.viewingTip: Sit quietly near a talus field and scan with binoculars for movement — pikas overheat easily, so never linger long enough to keep one from returning to its haypile.
animals.didYouKnow: Pikas don't hibernate; instead they spend summer gathering 'haypiles' of dried vegetation to survive on under the snow all winter.

animals.whereToLook: Forest edges and meadows throughout the park, including Longmire and Ohanapecosh
animals.viewingTip: View from the road or trail with binoculars, especially during the November rut when bucks are more on edge — never approach for a closer photo.
animals.didYouKnow: Columbian black-tailed deer are a subspecies of mule deer found only along the Pacific Coast from California to British Columbia.

animals.whereToLook: Dense forest at lower and mid elevations; rarely seen
animals.viewingTip: Sightings are extremely rare; if you encounter one, keep children and pets close, make yourself look large, and back away slowly instead of running — never approach or try to photograph it up close.
animals.didYouKnow: Despite roaming the entire park, mountain lions are so elusive that many rangers who've worked at Rainier for decades have never seen one in the wild.

animals.whereToLook: High-elevation trailheads and campgrounds like Paradise and Sunrise
animals.viewingTip: Gray jays are famously bold around hikers, but resist the urge to hand-feed them — human food harms their health and habituates them to approaching people for handouts.
animals.didYouKnow: Also called the 'camp robber,' the gray jay caches thousands of food items each year, gluing morsels to tree bark with sticky saliva for winter.
